articles.title: UNIONISTS AND NON-UNIONISTS.
articles.text:
UNIONISTS AND NON-UNIONISTS.

I HAVE been writing for some ten years in
the BEE-HIVi . and elsewhere on the subject
of so-called coercion and intimidation by
Trades Unionists, and I dare say readers, as
well as writers, would have been thoroughly
weary of it by this time were not its impor-
tance continually being brought home to us
by the decisions of our tribunals. So long as
Mr. BRUCE'S Criminal Law Amendment Act
remains unrepealed, we 'are not likely to be
left 'without substantial reasons for reeurring
to the well-worn theme. Since I wrote on
it last week, the Hammersmith case has added
one more illustration of the unjust and
tyrannical principle embodied in that
Act. However sorry we may be that
Mr. TURK should suffer so much discomfort
and trouble, we cannot affect to regret that
employers should be found vindictive and
short-sighted enough to put the law in motion,
and magistrates who are ready to give it the
severest interpretation. It is best that work-
men should know at once to 'what they are
liable, and that the agitation against the
recent Act should begin before they have
forgotten the name of the Minister who carried
it, and carried it with the full knowledge of
the way in which it would be worked. If the
conviction of Mr. Tuna: is affirmed, and he has
to serve his time in prison, let us have a
public subscription to make him some com-
pensation, and let us give him a public dinner
when he comes out, in order to show that in
the opinion of many of his fellow-citizens he
has done nothing of which he need be ashamed.

" The Trade- Union Act' of last session
was a good measure, and we may see how much
wai gained by separating it from the "Criminal
Law Amendment Act." Our opponents, too,
have found out that we stole a march on them
there, and are bekinning to exclaim that they
were substantially one measure, and that if
the latter Act is to be recast, the former must
go into the melting-pot along with it. In
other words, if unionists will not submit to a
tyrannical and unjust law about molestation,
they shall have no protection for their funds.
But they need not be alarmed by this menace.
There are some things which once done cannot
easily be undone. Glaring abuses of vener-
able growth may linger on a long time under
Parliamentary government before they are
remedied, and if apowerful class has an interest
in their perpetuation, there are many well-
known ways of thwarting and impeding every
attempt to remove them. B ut when such an abuse
has once been swept away, because the public
conscience has come to regard it as too scan-
dalous to be tolerated any longer, there is not
much fear that the stop will he retraced.
Embezzlement of trade society funds has at
last been made ; and, though anonymous
journalists may propose to re-legalise it, there

is no probability that members of Parliament,
whose names are known, and who are re-
sponsible to public opinion, will venture on
any such step.
The Parliamentary enemies of workmen
always assume that there is a large non-
unionist body craving protection against
unionists. Ido not doubt that many middle-
class people honestly believe that this is the
ease. Those, however, who have taken pains
to inform themselves, are well aware that non-
unionists, as a rule, are very glad that there
are unionias to stand up for the interests of
their trade.

A non-unionist carpenter in London enjoys
the same wages as the society man, though ho
knows right well that without organization
the advanced rates of recent years would never
have been gained. The man who has a right
to feel sore is the unionist, who has to bear a
double burden because the non-unionist
shirks his share of it, while enjoying a
full measure of all advantages obtained.
From this point of view, I entirely
sympathise with the remarks of Mr. ALLAN
and Mr. °TULE at the Nottingham Con-
gress, with respect to workmen's clubs and
meeting rooms. If such institutions are to
succeed, they must be started and kept up by
men who have certain opinions and sentiments
in common, and must not be open to every man
who tenders his entrance fee, even though he
can prove his respectability. Those who
exhort workmen to sink their differences
and meet in the club as on neutral ground are
wanting in due respect for a very proper and
dignified feeling. Those workmen who tax
themselves, submit to certain wholesome rules
and possibly sacrifice their private advantage
for the good of their class, stand upon a higher
moral level than those who claim to do as they
like; and, no amount of patting on the back
from middle class patrons, can compensate the
latter for the displeasure of their fellows, which
they feel they deserve.
E. S. BEESLY.

A MODERN STATESMAN.

THE Earl of DERBY is a model statesman.
He is sedate and unimpassioned. He never
abuses his opponents, nor greatly overstates his
case. He knows what can be said on both
sides of every disputed question, and seems
only to take the Conservative rather than the
Liberal view, because it would be indecorous in
so:moderate and sensible a person to shock any-
body's feelings by doing what nobody expects
him to do. With so general a faith in com-
promises as we have in England, it is in the
very nature of things that his speeches should

NORTH STAFFORDSHIRE.
IRONWORKERS AND COLLIERS.

The men employed in the mechanical depart-

fordshire have had a meeting, at which great
satisfaction was expressed at the concession of the
nine hours system recommended by the Iron and

been made, a resolution was passed requesting

Tyne.

ISLE OF WIGHT.
THE NINE HOURS MOVEMENT.

The nine hours movement has at last been set
on foot in the Isle of Wight, and the first firm to
adopt the nine hours system, as far as we can hear,
is the Isle of Wight Railway Company, the pro-
prietors of which have voluntarily consented to
give the working engineers employed at their
works in Ryde the benefit of the nine hours move-
ment, The new arrangement commenced on
liaturday, when, headed by a brass band, the mon
paraded the streets of Ryde, each carrying a
polished section of a railway engine. We under-
stand it is the intention of other firms in the island
to follow the example of the railway company in
this respect.

WOLVERHAMPTON.

ME IRON TRADE.

At a conference of masters and men held at
, Wolverhampton on Wednesday the masters sub-
mitted the following proposition to the men
"That the standard rate of paddlers' wages shall
be based upon a scale of 10s. per ton; that such
advance or reduction of 20s. a ton in the price of
bars shall be met by an advance or reduction of
ad. per ton in the price of puddling. The mill-
men's wages be fixed upon the proportionate scale
now existing as compared with puddlers wages,
and shall be subject to an advance or reduction
of 5 per cent., with such advance or reduction
of 20s. in the price of bars. That the selling
price of iron shall be ascertained by a sworn
accountant, who shall examine every six months
the books of 12 members of the iron trade; and
the average selling price for' the last six months
shall govern the price of wages for the following
six months. That the rate of puddling shall be
10s. per ton, from and after the first Monday in
February to the end of June next, and that the
average price at which iron has been sold in April,
May, and June shall govern the price for the next
six months."

Meetings of the men will bo hold to consider
the proposal.

THU CIENERAL UNION Or CAIIVENTERS.

In the forty-fourth annual report of the above
Society, Mr. 11. Last, the Secretary, speaks as
follows :
Turning from other topics to matters closely
connected with General Union, it will be seen, on
reference to the annexed report, that we now num-
ber 126 lodges, with 7,432 members, showing a

nution in the number of lodges having occurred at

The expenditure on all sources, during the year
and a quarter included in this report is £11,046
4s. lid., being £6,080 Bs. 6id. for what are known

as trade purposes; 3,025 15s. 7d. for sick and
superannuation benefit, and £l,OlO on funeral and
aocident account. It is gratifying to observe that.
this outlay is less by £2,114 ss. 9d. than the
amount given in last year's report. This wel-
come fact is traceable to the very small disburse-
ment upon strikes, which reaches the merely
nominal sum of £331 2s. 3d; and the greater
portion of the amount expended, therefore, has
been applied to the benevolent and other beneficial
objects of the Society. Thus, for instance, £3,925

15s. 70. has relieved those of our brethren in times
of sickness, or who, on account of advanced age,
and vmsequont incapacity to follow their em-
ployment, are receiving superannuation benefit.
£l,lOO Is. 3d. has been absorbed by those out of
employment through iuckunent weather or depres-
sion of trade, whilst many, seeing no immediate
propect of resuming work in their own localities,
ha vo migrated to more favoured spots, and been
assisted with the funds for travelling purposes to
the extent of £145 13s. 100.

Tools purloined during the year have been re-
placed by the Union subscribing £7l is. Id. As
has been the case for the last few years, the
liabilities for making good tools destroyed by fire
are extremely light, inasmuch as £BO 1 Is. 4d.
covers the whole demand.

:Death has, however, been busy in our ranks,
hawing deprived us of 75 members, at a cost of
£750. The deceased wives of members, to the
n umber of GO, have entailed a further expendi-
turo of £24.0 ; while one of our craft who unfor-

innately injured Lis foot, resulting in amputation,

has been awarded £5O, as a soothing balm in his
taidortuue, i.9.ualuing outlay hehig uni,le up by

payment of officials, printing, postage, deputations,
and many small items, given in detail in the sub-
joined pages.
In closing my remarks, allow me to say that I
firmly believe the Union is now in the right track,
and that the check we have experienced may be
regarded as merely temporary. That we have been
pursuing a downward path for the last two or
three years has been self-evident. The signal
light, however, has at length been seen, the course
averted, and with our newly-trimmed constitution
there appears every probability of future success.
I feel that we are entering upon a new era in the
history of the Society, and that our progess
mainly depends upon the hearty co-operation of
the members at large. Let thorn be continually on
the alert in endeavouring to strengthen the hands
of the Executive Council in conveying sugges-
tions, through their lodger, as to any way in which
the Society may be extended and otherwise
benefited, and all join unitedly, and with a right
good-will, in an endeavour to push on the car of
progress, so that, great as has been the amount of
good conferred by the Society upon its members
in bygone years, it may yet be raised still higher
in its sphere of usefulness, and in its position
amongst the kindred institutions of the land.

articles.title: SOIREE or THE TRADES.
articles.text:
SOIREE or THE TRADES.

On Saturday evening a soiree was held at the
Broadmead-rooms, Bristol, to celebrate the granting
of the nine hours system in the workshops of the
city. The soiree had been postponed in consequence
of the illness of the Prince of Wales. There was
a large attendance.
Mr. K. D. Hodgmon, M.P., addressing the meet-
ing, said, in reference to the nine hours movement,
that it appeared to him that Bristol stood pre-
eminent in the admirable way in which it bad or-
ganised and carried it out. The workmen and the
employers had settled the question—one of the
most difficult in the world—in the moat amiable
and amicable manner, and having settled the
matter, they had not proeeeded, as he was sorry to
say some persons had done, to spoil almost the whole
of it. He adverted to the convictions of working
men for coercion at Bolton and in London, and
said in the latter ease an appeal would be made
against the sentence, aud he had no doubt it
would be as successful as the Bolton one wag.
Having denied that there was any such thing as
a natural antagonism between employer and em-
ployed, and having shown that the interests of
capital are not contra-distinguished from those of
labour, he went on to remark that he had heard
that there was an agitation being got up in favour
of the wotking hours being reduced to eight hours
per day. He advised his hearers to try the nine
hours system first. He urged his hearers to spend
the additional hour of leisure which they had
gained by doing good. In conclusion, he expressed
his admiration of the conduct of the employers and
employed in this movement.
Mr. S. Morley, M.P., expressed his belief that
there ought to be no antagonism between labour
and capital—that the interests of the employer
and the employed were mutual, and it would be a
blessed day for England and all classes in it when
that principle came to be understood. There had
been a ilisposition on the part of some to hold out
the two classes as standing in a position of an-
tagonism to each other. Now, he had good reason
to believe that they were coming nearer together,
getting to know each other, and ho was sure as
they did that they would feel more confidence in
each other. Ho was satisfied the nearer the two
classes came together, the more they had oppor-
tunities of conferring over the rights of each class,
the more harmonious would be the action between
employers and employed. Passing on to the nine
hours movement, he said the capitalists would get
better and more efficient service from their men
under the new system than under the old. He
was sanguine that this nine hours system would be
little, if any, loss to the employers, because he
believed in nine hours the workman who gave his
time and labour with the conviction that he had
been fairly treated, would do as much work, aye,
and do it better than the man who was compelled
to work ten hours under a helm of injustice and
unkindness. (Cheers)

LIVERPOOL.
TUE COACU UAKEUS.

As a constant reader and purchaser of the Bet-
Htve,l take the liberty of asking you to be kind
enough to publish the following :—To the Mute-
Coachbuilders of Liverpool and its vicinity.—The
committee of the Liverpool Operative Coach-
makers' Nine Hours League return their sincere
thanks to all those employers who have so kindly
conceded the nine hours to their workmen. They
also desire to acknowledge the courtesy shown
them while agitating the movement, and hope the
goad feeling at present existing between employers
and employed may so continue as to lead to their
mutual advantage.—By order, D. MINK; Secre-
tary." The coachbuilders of Liverpool have been
agitating for the nine hours, and have met with
great success,. On the Ist of January, 1872, 28
firms commenced working the 64 hours per week;
they work from 6 a.m. to 6 p.m. for the first five
days of the week, allowing half an hour for break-
fast, and one hour for dinner; on Saturdays they
work from 6 a.m. to 1 p.m., allowing half an hour
for breakfast. There is one firm that has not yet
()encoded the time, but they have promised to give
it the same day it is given by the London coach-
builders; from what we have hoard we believe the
London employers are favourable to the nine
hours. It is a great pity that our fellow crafts-
men in London should be divided, as they are, into
o many small clubs, which are almost powerless
by themselves when agitating any great question,
such, for instance, as the reduction of the hours of
labour; instead of taking this lead on all groat
questions affecting the trade, they are always be-
hind hand. When the Saturday half-holiday was
gained by tho workmen in most of the large towns
In the provinces, the men in London were content
to work on at the old hours for some years ; and
when they did go in for the Saturday half-holiday,
it was in such a half-hearted sort of way, that
their employers only conceded them four o'clock,
Instead of one o'clock, on Saturdays. It is to be
hoped the men will be wiser this time, and unite
all together, society and non-society, and form
One large society, or join the United Kingdom
Society; if they do this, they will, at no distant
date, beenabled tolead the van on all the groat ques-
tions affecting their trade, instead of following in
the wake of the leading towns in the provinces.
Lot them unite at once with a cordial good will,
and agitate for the nine hours, and lose no time
about it; and in the present temper of their em-
ployers they will, in a very short time, gain all
they ask for.

THE CONVICTION OF A STONEMASON
FOR MOLESTATION QUASHED.

At the conclusion of the criminal business at the
Bolton sessions, a case of considerable importance
to trades unionists came on for hearing. It was
an appeal by a stonemason named James Wearden
against the decision of the magistrates of this
borough, under the Criminal Law Amendment
(Violence, Threats, ece.) Act, ordering him to be
imprisoned for one month for having molested
another stonemason named Thomas Cooper, by
besetting the place where he worked, with a view
to coerce him, ho being a workman within the
moaning of tho Act 34 and 35 Victoria, cap. 32,
to pay to the Friendly Society of Operative Stone-
masons a fine of ss. Mr. Leresche and Mr.
Hopwood appeared for the appellant, and Mr.
Edge for the respondents.
The Recorder presumed that all formal notices
would be admitted F

Mr. Edge said ,he was instructed not to take
any objection, but to have the case heard upon its
merits. The case had attracted a vast amount of
attention out of doors, but with that they had
nothing to do. Whether it was policy or not that
there should be such a clause in the Act as that
under which the appellant had been convicted,
it was not for them to discuss, but they wore
there to decide whether the man Wearden had
contravened an Act of Parliament which was
passed last session. It appeared that both Cooper
and Wearden were members of the Operative
Stonemasons' Society, and on the 2nd August
last, when this offence was alleged to have been
committed, they were working together under Mr.
James Martin, builder, who had contracted for
the erection of a chapel. Wearier' was shop
steward of the society, and Cooper having in-
fringed some rule of the association, he was fined
55., which it became the duty of Wearden to
collect. Accordingly, on the date named, he went
to Cooper, and tendered to him a card upon which
appeared this fine. Cooper said, "All right; " but
Wearden remarked, "I want ss. from you."
Cooper replied, "I can't pay you." Wearden
told him he might get the money from the fore-
man, to which Cooper answered " I shall not get
it, for I don't intend to pay the fine." Wearden
then wont away, and he (Mr. Edge) believed re-
turned to his work. Had the matter ended there,
possibly there might have been no offence cont-
!flitted. Ho did not think it necessary to argue
that there was any offence up to that time, but the
whole case turned upon what was done subse-
quently. In the course of the forenoon Weardon
went to the foreman, James Clague, also a mem-
ber of the Stonemasons' Society, and represented
to him that Cooper would not pay this tine, and
that the other men had an objection to continue to
work on the premises with hint. Ho believed
Clugue was asked to discharge the Mall, but that
he refused to do so, and referred Wearden to the
master, who was not at that time present. Wear-
den went back to his work, and shortly afterwards,
seeing Mr. Martin with the foreman, he went up
to him, and made a similar representation to that
which he had already made to Clague. He said to
Mr. Martin, "There is a man upon the works who
is objectionable to us." Mr. Martin asked who it
was, and was told it was Cooper. He then asked
what was the matter, and he (Mr. Edge) thought
he was informed that Cooper refused to pay a tine.
Mr. Martin said, " Will you let the matter wait
till Saturday, and then I will discharge the man
Wearden made no reply, but walked away. The
men on the job, who were also members of the
society, worked until noon, when they left for
dinner. What took place during the dinner hour
he (Mr. Edge) was not in a position to say ; but
instead of resuming work at one o'clock, at they
ought to have done, they packed up their tools,
and went away, Cooper leaving the place at the
same time. Some time after that, Clague wont to
Cooper's house, paid him his wages, and said
something whieh might or might not be evidence
against Wearden, and on the following aaorninz

were the facts of the case.

Mr. Leresche then proceedad to a Idress the
court fur the appellant, observing that this act had
created a great sensation throughout the country.
It was vital, and would supersede the legislation of
previous sessions. There had been a great struggle
on the part of trades unionists to get their claims
recognised as lawful. At one time, combinations
were considered, per se, to be illegal, because they
were combinations to effect unlawful objects. But
the law was a meliorated so that workmen might
be allowed to combine for certain objects. But
while these associations were made lawful in the
sense that their members were not outlaws, still
they did not possess certain facilities which were
given by the Friendly Societies' Act and others of

the same kind. The reason of that was because
it was supposed they combined against certain
matters of public policy, as the restraint of trade,
and things of that kind. But the Legislature last
session, which passed this particular Act, abso-
lutely legalised all these societies, and declared
that they should not be unlawful by reason of
those particular matters, and it gave power to any
body of men to associate as a trades union for the
carrying out of objects which might even be con-
sidered a restraint of trade, and to register them-
selves as a friendly society.

remedy, and that we must not allow either our per-

its leniency to induce us to strain its terms either on
one side or the other for the purpose of bringing
within it or excluding any particular class of cases.
Now, looking at the phraseology and the terms of

SATURDAY, JANUARY 20, 1872.

THE CRIMINAL LAW AMENDMENT

ACT.

Oun readers will, in another column, see the
report of a case of considerable importance to
tradeunionists, which was heard at the Quarter
Sessions for Bolton, on Friday. It was an
appeal by JAMES WEARDEN, stonemason,
against a sentence of one mouth's imprison-
ment for having molested another stonemason,
named THOMAS COOPER, by besetting the place
where he worked, with a view to coerce him to
pay a line of ss. to the Operative Stonemasons'
Society. The conviction was under the new'
Criminal Threats Act. The men were work-
ing under Mr. JAMES MARTIN, builder, and
'WEARDEN, who was shop steward for the
society, went in working hours to collect the
fine from COOPER, who refused to pay.
WEARDEN then returned to work, but at
noon ho represented to Mr. MARTIN that a
man was on the job who refused to pay his
fine. Mr. MARTIN wished WEARDEN to let
the matter stand over until Saturday, and
then he would discharge the man. WEARDEN
made no reply to that, and after dinner the
whole of the men struck work. The foreman
afterwards paid COOPER his wages, and on the
following morning, the mon resumed work.
The RECORDER held that there had been no
molestation or besetting within the meaning of
the act. What the Act of Parliament intended
was to make illegal the system of picketing,
and he could see no resemblance between this
and what WEAUDEN did. He added, "I am
quite clear that the more application for the
payment of a fine, even though that were
immediately followed by an application to the
master to discharge the workman, could not be
said to be a besetting of the place within the
third sub-section," He therefore quashed the
conviction.

THE MEMBERS FOR BRIGHTON
BEFORE THEIR CONSTITUENTS.

As February draws near, the speeches of
members to their constituents multiply. Too
many of them are miserably colourless. This
circumstance indicates a lukewarm sense of
responsibility, a backsliding indifference,
forming an argument for parliaments shorter
than a whole apprenticeship. Of these defi-
ciencies, however, such men as the members for
Brighton cannot be accused; nor, when we
consider the original character of that town,
can we be otherwise than struck with adinira-

tion at the spirit of animation which, in poli-
tical respects, marks the bulk of its inhabi-
tants.

They are evidently well satisfied with their
representatives, and they have reason. TWO
men more independent, and at the same time
thoroughly Liberal, do not sit in the House.
With the exception of the Ballot Bill, which
he hopes to see reintroduced and passed in an
improved form, Mr. WnrrE, happily restored
to health, looks to a session chiefly occupied
with social questions; but then his view of
that epithet comprises such matters
Mines, Licensing, and Truck, on each of
which he is one to demand measures which
shall really protect the health and safety of
those who live in the bowels of the earth, shell
promote temperance, without perpetrating
injustice, and shall compel the payment of
weekly wages in solid coin. In this sponta-
neous echo of the voice of the Trades Congress
at Nottingham, he includes a call for the re-
vision, if not the repeal, of the Criminal Law
Amendment Act. On the subject of educa-
tion, he joins rank with those who mean t°
exact from the PRIME MlNisnat, unless he
prove blindly infLxible, a revocation of those
clauses in Mr. FORSTER'S Act which play into
the hands of the denomination schools, espe-
cially those in connection with the National
Society of the Established Church. Mr.
GLADSTONE will understand the hint that if,
instead of yielding to the expostulations of
his own supporters, he allows the heads of the
Church of Rome in Ireland the full benefit of
the same obnoxious principle, he must not
expect to be followed into the division lobby
by Mr. WHITE, even though the consequence
of his declining to do so should be a Minia-
terial crisis; not that the senior member for
Brighton exaggerates the importance of his
single vote. He is but one of many who share
the same determination, and he sat down,
mentioning the name of another, whose speecb
and vote will he both faithfully given, and
exemplarily regarded—Joux Baia RT.

The great importance of' setting right pre-
cedents was well pointed out by Mr. FAWCETT.
Do for us, say the Catholic prelates in Ireland,
at least as much as you have done for the
denominational schools in England. If, say
Ministers, you want to know what we have
done, look at our Irish Church and Irish Land
Acts. Very well, the Cambridge PROFESSOR
replies, do the same things for England, to
which they are equally applicable, and. in
which they are scarcely less needed. What-
ever distinctions may be drawn between the
Church disestablished on that side of the
channel, and the Church still established on
this, the English Dissenters of all kinds form
the larger half of the population; and the
general arguments on which establishment or
disestablishment proceeds in:one island, cannot
but be as logically applicable to the other. It
is for Mr. GLADSTONE and his colleagues to
determine for themselves the policy they Will
pursue. Only we wish for his sake that it mai
always be both right and consistent. At the
head of a party which, as Mr. Wurrs de-
scribes it, begins with Lord ItARTINGTON and
ends in Mr. ODOEU, the ?RM.; MINISTER may
feel that prudent management is required;
but we hope that he will never suffer himself
to be drawn into a weak imitation of the
miller with his ass in a vain effort to pleaeing
everybotly, but will anticipate the moral of that
fable, by at once and for all "sticking to what
is best."

The consequences of taking a course not
founded on principle, but on some mere notion
of expediency, are well shown by Mr. PAW-
cErr. "A Government is never helped by
obsequious flattery and unreasoning subser-
viency. Two years ago a policy was pursued
which alienated the Nonconformists, end
secured the support of the Tories. At first
nothing could promise better. The Adminis-
tration was strengthened by the whole force
of the Opposition, and the eighty or hundred
so-called discontented Radicals and Noncon-
formists were night after night defeated by over'
whelming majorities. It did not require great
gifts to predict what would take place. The
disaffection of the Nonconformists graduaUT
assumed the character of a serious estrange-
ment. This rupture would of course be
promptly taken a(lyantage of by the OPPoli"

tion, who never relinquished, but simply sus-
pended, their hostility to the Government."
The PROFESSOR'S representation of the case is
perfectly correct; only needing this supple-
mentary observation, that, whereas, had the
Ministry gone with the Nonconformist section
of their own supporters, and against their
avowed opponents, they would have been
backed by the large towns whose voice those
Nonconformists speak; while, by acting as
they allowed Mr. FORSTER to act,
they merely played into the hands of
their opponents, who will repay them on the
first opportunity, by pushing them out and
jumping into their places.
But, as Mr. Etwcerr showed, England
wants a Land Bill as much as Ireland
wanted one. And here he made a
dalpablo hit. Why, he asked, is there
no prospect of due attention to such matters.
Reports in abundance, and facts without
number, prove that the rural population are
in a miserable state, that agricultural improve-
ment is everywhere retarded by insecurity of
tenure, and that landlords on every hand are
embarrassed by complications and hampered
by forced coaditions, But who is to draw the
bill which should meet these crying evils?
Sir JOHN DUKE COLERIDGE is 110 more to
blame, indeed, than the best of his pre-
decessors; but is it not a mere farce to call him
a law-officer of the Crown, who, having been
occupied for seventy days with a private suit in
the autumn of the old year, is becoming still
more engrossed with the same matter, and it
may be for more than seventy days more,
within three weeks of the parliamentary
session, during which, by a farcical hypo-
thesis, he is supposed to be wholly engaged
In the Parliamentary service of the Crown!
Mr. FAWCETT might well ask, should we have
Dad the Irish Church and Irish Land Bills if
Mr. GLADSTONE, instead of devoting himself
to the preparation of those measures, had
placed himself at the head of some great
private trading establishment, the manage-
ment of whose affairs was sufficient to occupy
the whole attention of the most energetic
man?

articles.title: INTERNATIONAL ARBITRATION.
articles.text:
INTERNATIONAL ARBITRATION.

THERE is every prospect that Mr. HENRY
Run Ann's intended motion for International
Arbitration in place of war, will be made
under happy and promising auspices. The
voice of the country is being strongly and
generally lifted up in its favour. From several
parts of Europe important expressions of
sympathy are being given. The appointment
of International Arbitrators to meet at Geneva,
under the treaty between Great Britain and
the United States, has excited much attention.
In Spain, Senor MAncoinnr has given notice of
his intention to introduce a motion very similar
to that of Mr. RICHARD. In Sweden also, M.
HEDLUND has spoken and written much on
the subjeot. In France it is being discussed
In public journals, and a new Society for In-
ternational Arbitration Is being founded. In
Holland the Peace League have sent an ad-
dress to Mr. RICHARD. Its president is Hoer
Joule, of the Hague, a jurist of European
reputation, and now Minister of Judie° for
the Netherlands. Amongst its other leaders
are two Councillors of State—Hear J. P.
BACIIIINE and Dr. BLEENER—and five seem-
hers of the Dutch Parliament. "The General
League of Peace in the Netherlands," they
say, "testifies its sympathy with you for hav-
ing at this moment, when peace is not menaced
and the minds of men are again calm, taken
the initiative and at the same time the first
practical step in the way loading to the reform
of International Law."

LORD ELIOT ON POLITICAL BISHOPS.

Taa Earl of ST. GERMANS is patron of three
church livings, and is, we believe, free with
his money and land for church purposes. This
gives interest to the sentiments expressed on
such subjects by Lord ELIOT, his eon and heir.
In a lecture at Plymouth the other evening, he
strongly deprecated the presence of bishops in
Parliament, as tending to their secularisation;
as fostering the idea that the Church was a
Department of State, and as an argument
against the increase of the Episcopate. A seat
on the Right Reverend bench was too corn-
Inely a resting place from the fatigues of a

THE B

political stumping expedition. Bishops were
constantly exposed to obloquy, if they took a
line opposite to the majority outside, or, what
was worse, were tempted to vote from expedi-
ency rather than conviction. The necessary
absence from their dioceses was a convenient
excuse for the neglect of spiritual duties by
bishops politically-minded. The cove d'ilire
was also a monstrous abuse; but if the Crown
was to nominate bishops; in was well to reduce
to a minimum, the temptation to prostitute
powers. In short, he hoped, ere long, to see
bishops removed from a position detrimental
to themselves and injurious to the Church.

articles.title: PRANCE IN NEW PERIL.
articles.text:
PRANCE IN NEW PERIL.

TIIE fourth half-milliard of the war in-
demnity to Germany is being duly paid by the
French Government. M. THIERS maintains,
however, that, if the whole is ever to be forth-
coming, it can only be by the imposition of
duties upon raw materials entering France
from other countries. He is told that the
treaties entered into by her with foreign
powers, do not allow of the imposts which his
Finance Minister proposes. The answer of
the PRESIDENT of the REPUBLIC to this argu-
ment is not such as it ought to have been. In
fact, he does not face it, unless he can be con-
sidered as having done so when ho said that
"England had raised no objection of the kind.'
He did his own cause quite as much injustice
as he did the States of Europe when he accused
opponents of his course as "putting argu-
ments into the mouth of diplomacy." They
are sympathetic, no doubt, in their acknow-
ledgment that France is hard put to it to
restore the disturbed balance of her finances ;
but this by no means shuts them up to an
approval of the means by which the equili-
brium is sought to be brought back. This is
not the only proof thatM. TRIERS is perplexed
and losing his temper. He went so far on
Monday as to speak of the treaties of 1860 as
being of a fatal, detestable, and intolerable
nature; all the while knowing, as everybody
may see, that the commerce of France, which,
in the long run, must decide the action of
(Aland States, dreads and deprecates
nothing so much as it fears and forbids a
return to Protectionism. The present dis-
cussion has elicited no other fact so plainly
and so prominently as this. We shall see, at
the close of the debate, which M. TRIERS
would fain have cut short on Monday,
whether better arguments have occurred to
him than any urged at intervals, or even
during his famous three hours' speech. A
more oratorical triumph on a question of fiscal
policy, is a very unsatisfactory thing. Soft
sentiments and senile emotions are here
out of place. These railway and steamer
times are not those in which the
manufacturers of any country can be per-
suaded to believe, that, so long as their
fabrics are good, the price at which they are
offered makes no matter. The fact is, that
M. THIERS, and the party who are making him
their tool, not to say their throat-cutter, have
undertaken to turn back the tide; and there
can be no doubt what the tide will do with
them. No sooner does M. PonYER-QuERTIER
propose protection than the Rurals find one of
their own number to bring in a bill of exclu-
sion. Raw materials, in whatever bottoms
they come, are to be heavily taxed; and,
whenever they come in a foreign ship, or any
such ship carries away French produce, the
carriers are to pay three francs on every kilo-
gramme they take on board, and the ships
are to pay a largo amount per ton for the
privilege of registry in French ports. All this
would be as though we should restore our corn
and navigation laws,

No wonder that the Chambers of Commerce
join with the manufacturers of France in
earnest deprecation of measures ruinous as
well as retrograde. Under the system madly
sought to be set aside, the imports of France
have increased amazingly, and for her produce
and fabrics new or enlarged markets have been
found on many a coast. This is what M. TIIIERS
would reverse out of a tender patriotism, and for
reasons well worthy of the pretence. "Let
us discourage," be says, "those fine, large,
swift, and punctual British vessels, and then
our old, slow, and lazy tubs will have it all to
themselves." Such a policy, enforced with
such reasons, has well been compared to M.
IlAsnat's ironical representation of the can-
dle-makers as petitioning the Legislature to
prohibit and put out the sun.
M. TurEns and the lturals, under plea of
pursuing a resuscitating course, are, on the
contrary, driving despondency into despair,
and aggravating depression into ruin. The
single proposal to lay a special tax on commo-
dities taken from bonded warehouses aims a
deadly blow at French manufactures. In a
memorial to the Assembly by shipowners of
Bordeaux, it is affirmed that the proposed
additional taxes on goods imported under
foreign flags, and on warehousing, will not
only impose four millions sterling upon France,
but also destroy her mercantile marine. Tran-
sactions are conducted by telegraph, and it
would become impossible for distant corre-
spondents to effect purchases on French
account if not at liberty to freight available
ships without distinction of flag.

THE MANCHESTER OUARDIAN
AND THE BEE-HIVE.

IN an article on the Trades Congress which
appeared in the Manchester Guardian on
Monday last, we find the following comment
on ourselves :
"In the last number of the BEE-HlVE—the
organ of the trada unions—we come upon the fol-
lowing passage: 'For some time now the working
men of the kingdom have, as a rule, where it was
possible, put by the arms of force, that their dis-
putes might be settled peaceably, after a fair ex-
amination into the facts of each case. Things aro
now very strongly tending in this direction, and,
if speeded by the good-will of the employing class,
we may soon hope to see the day when the
industry of England will suffer little interruption
from trade disputes, and when masters and men,
through the growth of friendliness and mutual
consideration, will work harmoniously in all their
undertakings, greatly to the advantage of each
other, and very much also to the advantage of the
nation in whose prosperity they are alike in-
terested.' This statement is a somewhat one-sided
one, but in its spirit we heartily concur. We
cannot but believe that the traditional jealousies of
the two classes are passing away. It has been
too much the habit of each to assume that any
proposition emanating from the other must neces-
sarily be extravagant or unjust. What is required
to put an end to this is that when any question
as to time or wages arises between them each
aide should dispassionately examine the circum-
stances of the other, and decide upon facts instead
of the prowptings of fear or impossible economic
theories."

THE FUTURE POSITION OF
EMPLOYERS AND EMPLOYED.

ACCORDING to the Tines, the largest and
most influential meeting of the employers of
labour over held in the metropolis assembled
at the Palace Hotel on Wednesday. It coin
prised deputations from every seat of industry
throughout England and Scotland. The de-
mands of the operatives having gone on from
10 hours to 9, and from that to 8 with an
intimation from Mr. SCOTT RUSSELL that that
was only a step to 48 hours per week, in
competition with 65 on the continent, masters
find it indispensable to form a defensive coali-
tion, and the Conference formed itself on the
spot into an Association of Employers to
arrange or resist the the demands of trades
unions and other combinations of workmen.
A statement was given in by each firm of
the number of hands in their employment, and
the aggregate proved to exceed 100,000 men.
The Conference, which is strictly defensive,
was very unanimous and enthusiastic, and
proceeded at once to settle their rules, in the
view of immediate action.
The meeting, as far as we understand it, is
to concert measures to at once oppose de pro-

gressive action of the men, and to form a
temporary defensive organisation amongst Ca
employers, which is to be turned as soon as the
state of trade will admit, to a powerful aggres-
sive society, that is to play havoc with the
unions of the men.

We hope that the employers will be con-
siderate in this movement, and not do any-
thing to bring about a renewed hostility
between capital and labour. Much has been
done to allay the ill-feeling which previously
existed, and it will be unfortunate for the
employers if they bring back the state of things.
They perhaps know their own affairs best, but
we warn them against any premature action,
as is indicated in the proceedings of their Con-
ference.

If they aro unwise in their generation they
must not complain of any action on the part of
men to Main, and if possible, improve their
present position.

H. Belly, who, in commencement, pointed out
some of the practical difficulties encountered in
attempts to carry into effect these important ob-
jects. Thus it would be seen that at the present
time, though they might build castles in the air,.
they were not habitable. But turning from
the question of the difficulties encountered in
endeavouring to obtain the establishment of these
institutions, the speaker went on to say that they
would enable them to gain knowledge and use
their political power more wisely, making them
better workmen, better husbands, better citizens,
and nobler men. (Applause.) But whether they
built or not, they could, at ull events, occupy
rooms in their own particular neighbourhood,
which would answer the purposes required. After
referring to them as an investment, and the
benefits attending them, Mr. Solly asked how long
working men would be dependent on the middle
classes in their undertakings? They would observe
that some of the artisans of London and Liverpool
had succeeded to some extent in getting halls and
club-rooms for trade societies to meet in, while
they had failed in Oldham and Manchester, be-
cause where they had succeeded, gentlemen of the
middle classes had assisted in promoting the object.
How long was this to continue? They did not
need the help of these gentlemen to establish such
trade concerns. Before concluding, he briefly pro-
pounded a scheme for the promotion and establish-
ment of these institutions. (Applause.)
Mr. HickinF moved, and Mr. Kane seconded the
following motion:
"That this Congress, having heard the paper of
the Rey. Mr. Belly on Social Clubs, endorses the
objects aimed at, and is prepared to recommend to
their constituents the adoption of the social scheme
propounded in the paper, as tending to promote
social reform."
Mr. W. Allan wanted to know whether those halls
were to be open to all workmen—society and non-
society men. If they were, they would be a dead
failure. (Hear, hear.) That was the reason why
they. / had failed as ho told Mr. Solly beforehand
they would do. Union men would not tolerate
non-unionists going to the same place, and profiting,
for instance, from a labour registration. (Hear,
hear.) On thin latter point he objected to the
course being taken by a new paper, called the
Labour News, copies of which had been forwarded
to the delegates. Its advertisements as to labour
vacancies were moat injurioua. (Hear.) It was easy
to talk of their meeting at publiehowes, but where
else had they been üble to meet? They could not
get schoolrooms, and neither the churches nor the
chapels were open to them. (Laughter
and applause.) It was only since the
passing of the Trades Tinton Act that they could
inse their money for such a purpose, They had

been forced into the publicbouses. (Hear, bear.)
But now they had the power, those be represented
were intending to build hells in severallarge places.
(Applause.)
The Rev. Mr. Solly said it wai for the trades
unions themselves to say whether the halls should
be open or exclusive, they were tho judges. As
to the Labour News, be had himself warned the
editor what was likely to result.
Mr. Guile said it was all very well for Mr. Say
to say that ; but the Labour News, which was in-
serting advertisements for labour in the very lo-
calities where their societies had men on strike,
was edited by one of the hon. secretaries of the
Artisans' Club Institute, Mr. Alsager Hill. (Ap-
plause.) How could they have anything to do with
a movement so originating.
Mr. Allan: I will propose as an amendment,
simply "That Mr. Solly's paper be received."
Mr. Macdonald hoped the Congress would
give no countenance to this scheme. There was
too much of the Colonel Maude spirit in it. (near,
hoar.)

Mr. Odger, after some remarks, proposed "That, in the opinion oi this Congress, trade
hails and social clubs are highly essential to the
interests of labour, as they tend to bring work;ng
men together in a msnner better calculated to fur-
ther their objects than other places now resorted
to admit of; this Congresg, therefore, cordially
advises every society to take the subject into im-
mediate consideration."
Both Mr. Allan and Mr. Kane were willing
to withdraw their propositions in favour of this ;
but, eventually, Mr. Allan's amendment, accept-
ing Mr. Solly s paper, was put and carried sepa-
rately, Mr. Odger's motion being afterwards passed
unanimously.

TRADES COUNCILS.
Mr. Gyles next read a paper on the above sub-
ject. After dwelling at length upon trades coun-
cils, the speaker, referring to trades' halls, said
surely if co-operative societies could build halls
and premises suitable for their business, trades
unions—which far exceeded thorn in numbers and
in capital—are in a position to do so too. (Hear,
hear.) Trades unions were equal to employers on
boards of arbitration, and was there any reason
why they should not be equal in the mutter of
public buildings in which to discuss the great
questions affecting them? Trades unions com-
posed of employers could meet in their Exchange
Halls and their private club-houses, and why
should not trades unions composed of workmen
meet in their trade halts? Bettor schemes than
the one there suggested might be devised for
carrying out the objects in view; but, at any
rate, let each one use his utmost endeavours to
carry out the most desirable object, that they might
be certain that if that was done in earnest they
should not he ashamed of the result of their
labour.
Mr. Nicholson moved—
" That this Congress considers that trades coun-
cils are necessary and useful, as providing the
means by the combination of a number of societies
into one body, for the consideration of disputes
that might arise amongst them, and also with the
view of watching the interests of labour gene-
rally, thus frequently conferring greater benefits
by the earlier settlement of differences than would
otherwise be attained by separate action."
The resolution, which was seconded by Mr.
Bailey, and supported by Mr. Stevens, was car-
ried.
REPRESENTATION OV LABOUR IN PARLIAMENT.
Mr. It. M. Latham read an exhaustive paper
on "The best means of securing the repro-
limitation of labour in Parliament." Mr.
Latham remarked that they now possessed
popular power. Still, , they had great pro
-
Menu, to solve, which would tax their wisdom,
patience, and strength, wherever their faculties
were exerted. (Hoar, hem.). The first and most
important thing to be considered was as to the
difficulties attending the new situation. It was
true that, at first sight, under these circumstances,
sending working men into Parliament did not
seem to contain much promise of good. Some
might any that it would only tend to promote
a bad system of class legislation, while others
might deny that working men could carry into
the House of Commons any information by which
the Legislature would be helped in the considera-
tion of important social questions. On behalf
of the Labour Representation League, he wished
to say that working men in Parliament would
possess, not a special faculty for legislation, but
special experience. (Applause.) From the.oondi-
ton of their life the experience of the workshop
was theirs. They were acquainted with the
inconveniences and difficulties of the poor man in
life, and also with the thoughts and aspirations of
men who had felt the pinch and had reasoned on
the remedy. (Hear, hear.) The presence in the 1
House of working men would do much to remove
the objection of social inferiority which had
hitherto degraded the working classes. He
advocated that working men should help them-
selves, and not hand over tneir interests to others,
for "(hod helped those who helped themselves."
They must put themselves in Is position to assert
their demands, otherwise they would never be
satisfied. They should move on with a unity of
purpose and force derivable from a wise and
careful discipline, seeking to arrive at a precise
understanding of the policy they were to pursue.
Their action must acquire all the force which was
to be derived from earnest action, and must seek
out, as their representatives, the truly competent
men in the ranks of labour who had studied and
understood those questions which might be re-
garded us vital by British workers. (Loud Ap-
plause).
Mr. Graham moved "That, having heard the
paper of Mr. Latham, this Congress accords its
thanks to that gentleman, and is of opinion that
the realisation of the principles set forth will
contribute to the well-being of the working
classes." (Applause). He expressed his entire
concurrence with the paper.
Mr. Macdonald briefly seconded the motion.
Mr. Dale said ho would not like it to go forth

that they, as a congress, allowed the expression of
such strong political feelings as bad been enun-
ciated without entering a protest against it.
(Hear, hear.) He thought that if they allowed
this, it would do them no good, but rather the re=
verse; and he therefore begged leave to move that
the paper read by Mr. Latham be not received.
(Rear, hear.) -
•Mr Nicholson seconded the motion.
__ __

I Mr. Mottershead supported the paper in ques-
tion, pointing out that the matter was not a poli-
tical one at all. After remarking on the length
of time during which the miners of the country
had vainly attempted to secure a proper recognition
of their interests, the speaker went on to say that
the present House of Commons was in every sense
of the word a moneyed House. Parties went
there for interested motives, and it was for this
and other reasons that he would support the reso-
lution. (Applause.)
Mr. Oilger said the least they could do was to
receive the paper. To say the least, it contained
matter which was worthy of consideration, and he
did not think they would he doing right in practi-
cally placieg a veto upon it. To consider a thing
was not, necessarily to accept it. (Hear, hear.)
The original proposition did not conunit them to
any specific action, but merely called upon them
to accept the paper, which he himself could do
with all his heart. (Applause.)
Mr. Shiner said the association he represented
appeared for the first time at this Congress, be-
cause it had been thought that extraneous matters
were introduced. Ito thought, however, that the
paper should be accepted, together with a vote of
thanks to the reader. (Hear, hear.)
Mr. Howell supported the motion that the
paper be received. It mattere 1 little what man
they sent to represent them, so bug as he was
well acquainted with the wants and interests of
the working classes. By this means they would
confer a benefit on the class generally. (Ap-
plause).
Mr. It. Applegarth said there could be no doubt
but that there were working men who would with
advantage represent in the House of Commons
the interests of the working classes. (Hoar,
hear.)
After some observations from Mr. Kane,
Mr. Halliday said as working men were con-
tinually expressing a desire in this direction, it was
time they endeavoured to do something. The
miners of the country, he might say, had deter-
mined to find money to send men of their own
order, who could properly represent them, to St.
Stephen's. (Hoar, hear.) He hoped that they,
as working men, would consider the question, and
would come to the conclusion that their interests
would be best served by having their own men to
represent them. Thus they would have a greater
and better safeguard against class legislation.
(Applause).
Mr. Broadhurst said they would not consider
whether a man they sent was Whig, Tory, or
Republican, so long as he was right on the labour
question. Ho called on the delegates not to be
misled by the cry of "no politics." (Hoar, hear).
• He believed that it was of vital interest that they
should unite in electing men to represent the
interests of labour, leaving out altogether the
question of politics. Until they suceeded in doing
so, he thought that their Congresses and other
measures would be of little effect. (Cheers.)
Mr. Walton wished to move, as a rider to the
resolution, "That this Congress accepts the paper
read by Mr. Lattaun, and hereby expresses its
strong conviction that the labour interest should
be directly represented in Parliament by working
men hest qualified to give expression to the wants
and wishes of the working classes, in order that
the interests of labour may have the same atten-
tion in the House of Commons as all the other
interests represented there; and the members of
the Congress hereby pledge themselves to urge on
the various societies the necessity of electing as
many working men as possible at the next election."
Mr. G. Potter, in seconding the motion just
made, thought it a far better expression of opinion
than either of the resolutions, and that they wore
more likely to get a unanimous vote upon it.
(Hear, hear). The subject should be as free from
political feeling as possible. Though he had for
several years advocated the direct representation
of labour in Parliament, he had never been op-
posed to the selection of any working man who
thoroughly understood the labour question, and
the combinations of working men, even if such
person were a Tory. (Hear, hoar). If Mr. Wood,
secretary of the Manchester and Salford Trades
Council, was opposed to himself in politics, still,
-
on the labour question he was thoroughly sound
and, if he had to discuss the question in Parlia,
went, ho would do Ho as many of themselves,
although they were Liberals and he was a Con-
servative. Let them not have any division on the
subject of labour reprosentation—(hear, hear.) He
was of opinion that the concentration of action by
trades wits only wanting to send at least a dozen
men to Parliament to speak for labour, for poverty,
and for the lifting up of the people, which would
be as much for the benefit of the country as any-
thing else that capitalists could desire. (Hear,
hear.)
Mr. Dale and Mr. Graham then withdrew their
respective propositions in favour of that of Mr.
Walton, which was unanimously adopted.
The proceedings of the Congress then closed for
the day.

SATURILLY'ii PROCERUINGS.
The slack attendance on B•iturday morning
showed that a number of the delegates had left
for their homes. The President (11r. Leatherland),
in opening the pruceedings, said they had much
business Wow them, and he suggested that the
papers in the list should be taken as read. (Hear,
hear.)

CRIMINAL LAW AMENDMENT ACT.
MT. Macdonald aPtid : Esrtter nt their proceed-
ings they had agreed to do what they could in
getting rid of that unjnst pteee of recent legislation
which so grated on the oars of working men—the
Criminal Law Amendment /tot. It WWI true the

"B lton case" had been disposed of, but at Ham-
mersmith, on Friday, a case even more glaring than
that at Bolton occurred. The real offence of the
man in this last instance was giving a tract, or a
plactrd, to a workman. With the question
whether the man was actually in prison or not,
they had nothing to do; any law which was
capable of being so used as an engine of oppression
ought, for that simple reason, to be repealed at
once. Let them appoint a Parliamentary Com-
mittee to urge forward those matters, and to watch
every measure before Parliament affecting them
specially. If that committee found that either the
Government or the Parliament were reluctant, let
them call another Congress, and bring a pressure
to bear on the House that it could not resist. 111
submitted two resolutions, as follows :
First,—That a committee be appointed by this
Coneresa, to be called the Parliamentary Com-
mittise, for the purpose of taking any action that
may be necessary to secure the repeal of the pent'
clauses of the Criminal Law Amendment Act, the
Truck Act, and the getting a proper Compensation
to Workmen Bill, and te watch over the interests
of labour in general in the proceedings at Parlia-
ment, the committee to continue in existence till
the next meeting of Congress; and that the
oommittee shall consist of five members, three of
them to be selected from the provinces and two
from London.
"Second,—That it be remitted to the con-
siituencies to see if they will make a levy at a
rate as per member, or pay voluntarily such a
sum to maintain the action of the committee ;
that the answer of the trades' councils of trades'
societies be returned to the secretary of the com-
mittee within four weeks from the close of the pro-
ceedings of Congress; so that the committee msy
take the action necessary to realize the objects of
the appointment." (Applause.)

PAIILIANIEVTAny COMMITTIM.
Mr. Packwood, of Manchester, wended the
resolutions.

It was here mentioned that the Committee of the
Congress, on the previous night, had passed A
resolution suggesting nine instead of five as the
number of such a committee. After a long
discussion this modification was adopted; and
ultimately the following delegates were selected :
Maws. Macdonald, Miners; Leigh, cotton
apinnera; Higham, Nottingham; Howell, London;
Halliday, Amalgamated Miners; Leatharland,
Nottingham; Kane, Ironworker.; Melting*
Nottingham; Thomas, Shoemakers' Society; aud
Mr. W. Allen, Amalgamated Engineers, of the
committee, WU added to the list.

CO-OPERATION.
The Hon. Aubemn Herbert, M.P., at the requrst
of the Chairman, then introdueed the question of
"co-operation."
After which, Mr. Abbott moved—
" That this Congress earnestly requests trades'
committees and working men senerally to adopt
and promote co-operation and industrial partuer-
ships, this, we believe, being the -best means of
obtaining a just and satisfactory method of ar-
ranging and adjusting from time to time an
equivalent for their labour."

-On being seconded by Mr. Slatter, it was un-
animously passed.
The Congress then proceeded to consider the
place of meeting for next year.
Mr. Allan proposed, and Mr. Bailey se-
conded :

"That the next meeting of Congress be held in
Leeds on the second Monday in January, 1873."
—Carried.
The Chairman then announced that they had
six papers remaining unread. It was agreed "to
accept them as read."

TRADES UNIONS AND TUE lIDITCATION ACT.
Mr. Bailey presented a paper of great length on
this topic, treating of the manner in which recent
educational legislation had affected the interests of
the working classes, and how far they should be
content with "what had been erroneously celled
the compromise or settlement of 1870." Admit-
ting that there was a compromise between the
sects or religious parties in the House of Commons*
there was none agreed to by the working classes,
and there was no one in the Hottee allthOtilled to
make any compromise on their behalf. What the
working classes desired to have—and, notwith-
standing the politieel blunder of 1870, known as
Mr. Forster's Act, they believed they would
eventually obtain—was a nationel system of
education as opposed to the 'present thiamine.
tional and sectarian system. The first operation
of the Elementary Education Act in its re.
dation to the working clams, was to increase
the rates and taxes for the purpose of pro-
pagating the doctrines of the English and
Roman Catholic Churches. Nor must they
forget to notice, either, the £600,000 voted
for building grants. While the homes of many of
their fellow-workers were poor and squalid, and
their children ill-fed and they were
called upon to contribute to the national taxation
for the purpose of erecting huildinp in 01014 largely at their cost hereafter, the baseness of pro-
selytism would be carried on. They were being
rated, therefore, to make bulwarks fur the Church
of England in her struggles with the advancing
Liberal thought of the time. Yet up to the present
time not a board school had been eateblishod.
not a child was being educated in a school
under the direction and menagement of the
representative, of the ratepayers; in some places*,
whilst large additional sums were tieing paid out ot
the public purse for school fees, there wore fewer
children attending school than there were before
the Act came into operation. The method of deal-
ing with free education under the Act was ILD
insult to the intelligence oi the working classes.
They contributed largely to the national taxation.
Enormous national endowments were devoted to
tho °attention of the upper and middle classes, and
yet, under the Act, before a working man cou a
obtain, even for six menthe, free educatien for his
child, he was compelled to go before a ash( ol
board and declare that he was a pauper, and soh-
init to examination and cro.e-examination as to his
means of of paying school fees. The Act tot only

created a wider gulf than before existed between
the workiug class and the middle class, but it
created new distinctions amongst the working
clauses themselves. Two men working in the same
shop and living in the samestreet, might be put upon
a wholly different:footing as to the payment of fees.
The difference in the circumstances of families, as
to health and number of children, would often
create those distinctions where there was no real
difference of class. Trades' unions themselves,
causing, as they often did, temporary loss of
'work, would become under the Act instruments
for the pauperisation of their members. Worse
than all, the Act was in that respect one for
encoursging a spirit of hypocrisy, servility, mendi-
(tansy, and subserviency. It was impossible to
lay down any rule except the one rule that educa-
tion should be a national right, free to all and
supported by all, and that compulsion should not
be used for the purpose of filling sectarian schools
and propagating sectarian doctrines.
No resolution was taken upon the subject.
CONVICT LABOUR.

Another paper was on the subject of "Convict
Labour," and Mr. Odger proposed :
"That this Congress views with serious appre-
hension the unfair competition which the intro-
duction of convict labour has created in the public
market, and is of opinion thit the disposal of such
labours should be confined entirely to the various
charitable institutions of the country."
The cocoa-nut matting trade, he said, had been
nearly ruined by prison authorities going into the
market and underselling the other manufacturers.
. This tended to increase pauperism, and even, it
might be, crime. (Hear, hoar.) By charitable
institutions, as mentioned in the resolution, he
meant their blind institutions, deaf and dumb asy-
lums, hospitals, the Army and the Navy, and, if
they liked, the police, all of whom wanted goods. If
the prison authorities would supply these institu-
tions at the cheap rates the better it would be for
the taxes, for the working men, and for the fair
employer in the open market.
Mr. Shipton seconded the resolution, and it was
carried.

INTERNA.TIONAL ARBITRATION.
The following resolution, proposed by Mr.
Cramer, and seconded by Mr. kane, was also
unanimously adopted :
" That this Congress rejoices to -learn that Mr.
IL Richard, M.P., has notified his intention to
move, dining the next session of Parliament, a
resolution in &your of the establishment of a
permanent system of international arbitration,
and trnsts that as the question is not one of a party
character, the House of Commons will rise to the
greatness of the occasion aid the urgency of the
subject., by giving a cordial support to Mr.
Richard's motion; and that copies of this resolution
be forwarded to the Premier, the Right Hon. B.
Disraeli, and Mr. Richard."
VT. Abbott moved:—

that the same might be able to remove the whole

The motion having having been seconded by
Mr. Mellen, was adopted.
AMALGAMATED SOCIETIES.

Mr. Crenaer moved an " instruction " to the
Parliamentary Committee which had been appointed,
as follows

" That, inasmuch as the tendency of trades
unions is to amalgamate and become national
rather than local, and as, owing to the decision of
the magistrates at the Marlborough-street Police-
court, in the case of the Amalgamated Society of
Carpenters and Joiners, such amalgamated bodies
are only unions in name; and further, as clause 9
of the Trades Union Act, which attempts to remedy
the evil, is ambiguous, it is forthwith resolved
that it ix) an instruction of the Parliamentary
Committee to use every exertion to obtain such an
*lteration in clause 0 of the said Act as to render
clear and definite theposition and power of branches
of amalgamated societies, and to make them what
their rules intend them to be—sections of one large
body."
Mr. Giles seconded the iesolution, which was
carried.
Resolutions thanking the president, vice-presi-
dent, !secretary, and the press were paused.
The proceedings of tho Congress then termi-
nded.
