WORKING MEN'S MEETING.

On Thursday night a meeting of working nun
was held in the Lecture Hall of the Mechanics'
Institution, Nottingham, and it was largely
attended.

The meeting was presided over by Mr. A. J.
Mundella, who observed that during the
week a Congress of considerable importance, so
far as the labouring classes of England were con-
cerned, had met in that room, and he must say on
behalf of the Conference that the Mayor and
Members for Nottingham had done what they
could to give them a most thorough and hearty
reception to that town. (Hear, hear.) The
gentlemen who were about to address them that
night were lenders of the working men, captains as
it were of the several branches of industry—men
who were veterans in championing the rights of
the working men. It would be bad taste on his
part to detain them with a long address, and he
thought he should be beat showing his appreciation
of their time and their appreciation of the
gentlemen who were about to address them,
by calling upon them to do so. (Cheers.)
Mr. George Potter moved the first resolution as
follows

_
"That, in the opinion of this meeting, trade
combinations afford the best means of securing to
the industrial portion of this country a just and
reasonable share in the results of their labour, as
well as the rectification of the grievances under
which they have long suffered." He said that
during the last few years trade unionists had
rapidly found reoognition by the Legislature and
the country. He did not know whether all pre-
sent belonged to trades unions, but he did know
this, that working men who did not belong to such
combinations, had indirectly received very im-
portant benefits from them. (Cheers.) He had
always contended it was the duty of the working man
to combine with his fellow working men to
mutually benefit their condition. "Unity was
strength," and they all know that a working man
singly had little chance of getting his wages
increased, his hours of labour reduced, whereas by
united action their requests had been generally
granted. (Mar' hear.) Hithei to the working
classes had not had a fair and equal share in the
profits of their labour, but he hoped the time woe
not distant when they would obtain some participa-
tion in the results of their work. He advised them
to endeavour to rake the condition of the lower
strata of the working classes, to seek to remove the
prejudices of the opponents to trades' unions, and
to take every fair means by their trade combina-
tions to gain a fair proportion of the profits of their
labour. On resuming his seat Mr. Putter was
loudly cheered.
Mr. Leigh (Manchester) seconded Mr. Potter's
motion, and pointed out the advantages of trades'
unions. He said in the trade to which he belonged
(cotton spinners), since the trades' union had been
established, the rate of wages had been increased
25 per cent. A further necessity of trades' unions
was to give relief to suffering brethren when out of
employment from sickness, or from any other
cause.
_ .

••.• ••••,1., •
Mr. M'Donald, of the Miners' Association, said
that he bad pleasure in meeting such a large body
of the workmen of Nottingham to speak to them of
the benefits of trades' unions. lie would cite
examples so far as his association was concerned,
showing that trades' unions were benefits as com-
pared with non-union districts. Their association
had during the last three years spent over £20,000
in benefits alone. In this they were at war with
the Bastile of England, and if the working men of
England followed their example, there would be no
Union Workhouse in existence, and men would be
in a position to maintain their own. (Cheers.)
They had another branch of their association in
Northumberland. In 1863 these men organised
themselves, and until 1870, while other non-
unionists had their pay reduced in some cases by
25 per cent., they never had any reduction at
all. The could give instances a this kind without
number. He was glad that he was in the town
of Nottingham, and congratulated his audience
in having more Boards of Arbitration than
any other town in the kingdom. Their town
might be called the home of arbitration, but if
they let union go arbitration would pass away like
a vision of the night. (Cheers.) If they wanted
freedom they must stick to the unions. If they.
wanted their unions to he respected they must
establish benefits, and so drive the %stile out of
existence, and got labour union established in its
place. (Loud cheers).
The lion. Auberon Herbert, M.P., was the next
speaker, and was most cordially received. Ile
said the great want of labour in the present day
was that of voluntary organisations. First of all
as to this groat matter of arbitration, as Mr. Rupert
Kettle had said, "the only hope of arbitration
begins where the unions are strong and well
consolidated." They wanted organisation, more-
over, when they passed out of the region of arbi-
tration. There were still left in this country
sonic great abuses which arbitration could not
reach; anti the only way, and the best way, in his
opinion, to deal with them was for them to join
together, to trust to their own force, and to make
one determined stand against them. (Hear, hear.)
Where such abuses existed, it was the duty of all
i
of them, he believed, who were interested n the
great labour question to go to that district, and to try
to rouse those who were suffering under the injustice,
so that they might form themselves into a union
to appeal on their behalf to the country; and, if
they could do anything else for them, at least
bodily to emigrate from that spot and suffering.
This was strong language, but he was speaking
of those great and terrible injustices which could
not be removed by such a mild measure as arbi-
tration; such an injustice was the truck system.
T.heir unions were also a measure of insurance to
them against times of sickness, relieving them on
occasion of illness and death, and bad trade.
(Loud cheers.)
Mr. Graham (stonemasons') remarked that, sin-
gular to say, the association which he represented
was established in the same year that he was
born—(e, laugh.) It sprung into existence in

Huddersfield, and be was prone' to tell them that
at the present moment the mations were united
together in otie grand organisation. (Cheers.)
They enjoyed many benefits, sonic of which were
optional; but they knew nothing of the truck
system. (Itenewed cheers.) They had Set their
faces against all indirect payments, stoppages, or
deductions; they 'wore paid, and promptly paid,
for the " job " wherever the contract was going
on. They had also agitated for the short time
movement, and succeeded in getting the hours of
labour reduced to nine hours per day. Courts of
arbitration were unknown in the trade, but be
wished to say the men invariably despised the
principle of unfairness, and he hoped they would
always despise it. The other day 'Mr. Samuel
Morley—(cheers)---a gentleman with whom be
had often been in communication on trade affairs
—referred to the question of labour, and said be
should like to hear something from the Congieas in
regard to its duties and obligations. (Hear, hear).
'Well, all that he could say in return was, that the
masons recognised their duties towards their
employers. (Hear, hear.) Englishmen generally
were distinguished for working with all their
might, and he was sure the masons were not
behind band; in fact, in the Western States of
America, he had known them almost work tketn.
selves to the grave. (Cheers.) With these re-
marks be begged most cordially to support the
resolution. (Cheers.)
Mr. It. Applegarth (London) gave a history of
the society to which be belonged. When he
joined the society there were but thirty-two
branches, with about £7O in funds, and now they
had 10,000 brunches, with funds amounting to
£20,000. But, better than that, their union had
tended to create a good feeling amongst workmen
in the kingdom, and to put down that internal
strife and jealousy that otherwise exists. Trades'
unions could be also used for political purposes. They
should not have had household suffrage but for
trades' unions. They should not have had Arbitra-
tion Boards, they should not have had their
present Education Bill were it not for trades
unions. But were they to be content with this ?
If they turned to the agricultural districts they
might give the advantages of their experience to
the agricultural labourer, (Hear, hear). Was
it not a fact that they were increasing their
eonntry's wealth, whilst others were reaping the
benefits of the increase, He did not wish, how-.
ever, to say anything against the capitalist, for
it was the system that was wrong, and not the
people who lived under it. (Hear, hear). He
considered that, however much trades unions had
done in the past, it was nothing to what they were
capable of doing in the future if they would
put their shoulder to the wheel. Educa-
tion was at the bottom of it all. They must
edecate acid educate until they could put the
working man in a position to enjoy life in the
most enlightened form. (Cheers.)
Mr. J. Kane (Darlington) pointed out the
benefits which had resulted in his district from
arbitration. Ho would regard it as a calamity to
the trade he represented if their board were to
break down, but this, he was glad to say, was far
from likely. As to the truck system he thought
this would be put down by trades unions, for if
wages were paid weekly the system could not
live. (Hear, hear). If they could only prevail
upon all the societies to endeavour to establish
boards of conciliation and 'arbitration working
men's home comforts would be considerably
increased, and the fearful amount of pauperism
at present existing would be less known than,
unfortunately, it was now. Trades unions, he
would say, might do more than they were doing.
Why, he asked, should men living in counties be
deprived of the privilege of voting possessed by
men in towns? He hoped this would be remedied,
and that, with the co-operation of friends in
Parliament, they would be able to carry on
successfully an agitation in this direction. (Ap-
plause). When this was secured they would have
to regard measures, not men, and, whether Whige
or Tories, kneels loudly at the door of St. Stephen's
and say, "These reforms are necessary, and we
must have them." (Loud applause)."
The resolution was then put and carried unani-
mously with acolamation.
Mr. Highain (Nottingham), in noticing the
recent legislation as affecting trade societies, said
a petition had been drawn up on the subject which
it was suggested that the chairman should sign on
behalf of the meeting, in favour of the abolition
of the penal clauses of the Criminal Law Amend-
ment Bill. The petition ran as follows :
"That year petitioners, having taken in consi-
deration the results of legislation on trades
societies during the last session of Parliament, are
firmly of opinion that it
.has signally failed in
effecting the objects previously anticipated; that
the exceptional and vague character of the penal
clauses of the Criminal Law Amendment Act
establishes a new catalogue of law-created
crimes, which are aimed at workmen in combina-
tion, but when committed by other persons in an
individual capacity are not consideied
That with this view WO are strongly convinced
that the aforesaid Criminal Law Amendment Act
insidiously aims a blow at the liberties of' trade
organisations, whilst it has a tendency to foster
and strengthen a feeling of antagonism towards
workmen on the part of the employers. We there-
fore wish emphatically to declare our disapproval
of the aforesaid Act, and earnestly call upon your
honourable House to at once repeal the clauses
relating to coercion and molestation, and thus
place the members of trade societies on an equality
before the law in common with the rest of the
community; and at the same time we express our
fixed determination not to rat &Walled until this
has been accomplished."
, In conclusion, Mr. High= said there could be
, no doubt but that the measure was one which
pFessed very heavily upon them, and, under these
circumstances, he trusted that the chairman would
be inclined to endorse the petition on behalf of the
meeting. (Applause.) He moved accordingly.
Mr. Hieking (secretary of the Congress),- in
seconding the proposition, wished to be allowed to

state that about a fortnight since some 80 men
left the employ of a certain firm in this town, tipon
which the firm by whom they had been enaployed
issued a document to the other employers in the
trade, saying that "their object in making the
conamunicatron was not to give countenance to the
proceeding, as they were assured that this case
was only the forerunner of other claims to be
made." More than this, a list of 75 names of the
men who had been'employed was given. (Shame.)
Now while these acts could be committed with
impunity by employers, it was the duty of
working men to obtain the repeal of the Criminal
Law Amendment Act. (Applause.) It should not
be forgotten that this was one of three or four
cases of a similar nature which he could name.
(Shame.)
Mr. Halliday (miner) characterised the Criminal
Law Amendment Act as an obnoxious specimen of
class or special legislation, but as the measure had
been passed it would be seen that the working
men of Nottingham and the country would raise
their voices and say that they would not counte-
nance such an Act, Ho would not say how their
members had voted, but, suppose one had voted
wrongly, let him be asked to re-consider his vote.
However they might act here, he could only say
that elsewhere they were determined not to retihn
such men unless they re-considered their vote. He
hoped that those who were not union men would
become union men, and those who were would
continue so. If they (lid, and took care to raise
themselves intellectually, they would not only im-
prove themselves, but, in addition, brighten the
future of the country. (Applause.)

in the Criminal Law Amendment Act, and said he
should not rest satiatled until they were repealed.
The unionists asked Parliament for bread, and they
gave them a stone; and, as the representative of
probably the oldest trades union represented on
the platform, he begged to protest against such a
proceeding. In 1810, the pioneers of his society
were compelled, when they had attended auniorrist
meeting, to take their spades and dig a hole in the
field in which to bury their books, for there was
not a single house that would have them. (Shame.)

day be singled out as a particular portion of the
community to which a particular Act of Pasha-
merit should apply? (Hear, hear.) They worked
as hard as any other body, and took as much care
of their money, and the reason they were singled
out was because the god of gold affirmed they must
be. (Cheers.) At the end of the year 1869, the
ironfounders had endured three years of the
greatest depression ; but sooner than see them
want for bread, the men whom be represented
weekly subscribed 2s. each from their earnings for
at least fifteen or eighteen months. (Cheers.)
Since that time things had changed, and he saw it
brighter day before them. In fourteen years the
three seeietiea mentioned by Mr. Applegarth had
paid for unemployed labour more than £lOO,OOO.
(Cheers.) In three years the ironfounders and
, engineers alone paid nearly £300,000. Did they,
he asked, deserve "black balling" for doing these
, things? (" No, no.") For benevolent purposes
of the purest kind they had paid in fourteen yearn
£1,113,927 sterling. (Cheers.) Was that no-
thing? What rates had it saved, and how many
a man had it kept out of the workhouse. (Cheers.)
Mr. W. 11. Wood (Manchester) said for year*
past they had endeavoured to free themselves from
class legislation. He could not now come to any
other conclusion than that those members of Par-
liament they had sent to represent them must haver
been strangely neglectful to have allowed the
measure of last session to become law. They
themselves would address Parliament in a respect-
ful manner, and be asked them now, as working
men, whether they would endorse that measure
or strengthen their hands by asking the Govern-
ment repeal such legislation? What they
aimed at was shnply to ask trades unionists
,to discharge their duties. But, favourable as ho
was to the shortening of the hours of hobeur, he
would not at this period do more than ask theta us
support the labours of Congress. (Applause.)
The resolution was unanimously_ carried.

On the motion of Mr. Macdonald, seconded by

passed to the Chairman and the Hon. Auberon.

Mr. Mundolla, in replying, said he thanked the
meeting on behalf of himself and his hon. friend
who had just left the platform. Ho would only
any that in taking part in the Congress during the
present week he had heard some opinions with
which ho did not agree; but he was never at a
Congress in his life—whether the Social Science
Congress of the British Association—at which he
did not find much with which ho disagree.
Still, he must say of the Congress during the pre-
sent week the tone throughout had been practical,.

only be solved by such intelligent meetings, and
especially by meetings of employers and employed.
As a Nottingham man he had great pleasure in
welcoming the Congress, and in showing them
every courtesy and hospitality, as he felt it his duty
to do so. (Applause.)
